title: Popular Roman preaching of ignorance clashes with the Schools’ moral certainty—FINIS Certitudine
source_text: LVI. Profecto non fert communis hominum, imo nec ipse Scholae usus, ut dicamus aliquem ignorare, dubitare, incertum & ancipitem esse, quum non solum vere, sed etiam firmiter & determinate judicat rem ita se habere, quanquam solum moralem, vel conjecturalem, habeat certitudinem. Quum vero dicitur quispiam dubius & incertus, sive rem aliquam nescire, statim concipimus illum inter utramque partem contradictionis haerere, nec quicquam circa id de quo quaestio est, determinate apud se judicare atque statuere. Quod manifestum est ipsa plebis Romanensis experientia. Quum enim assueta sit audire Doctores suos publice disputantes, & asserentes in suis apud eam concionibus, fideles ignorare an sint in Dei gratia, & nescire an Deus ipsos vel amet, vel oderit, eosque dubios & incertos esse, num revera adepti sint peccatorum remissionem, & justitiae donum, inde colligit fideles circa ista esse debere animo suspenso atque ancipiti, neque posse de istis firmum & determinatum apud se ferre judicium absque temeritate atque arrogantia: ac proinde pios & justos circa haec ne quidem habere certitudinem quam Scholae concedunt, nempe, moralem, sive conjecturalem. Et sic Scholae Romanae hac in parte dogmata, multum discrepant a sensu, quem ipsius Doctores, plebi ipsi auscultanti, praedicationibus suis ingenerare solent.
pass_a_gloss: Truly the common usage of people, nay even the usage of the School itself, does not bear that we say someone is ignorant, doubts, is uncertain and wavering, when he not only truly but also firmly and determinately judges that the matter so stands, although he has only moral or conjectural certainty. But when someone is said to be doubtful and uncertain, or not to know some matter, we immediately conceive that he sticks between both parts of a contradiction, and determines and settles nothing determinate within himself about that which is in question. Which is manifest from the very experience of the Roman populace. For since it is accustomed to hear its doctors publicly disputing and asserting in their sermons to it that the faithful are ignorant whether they are in God’s grace, and do not know whether God loves or hates them, and that they are doubtful and uncertain whether they have truly obtained remission of sins and the gift of righteousness, from that it gathers that the faithful ought to be of suspended and wavering mind concerning these things, and cannot make a firm and determinate judgment within themselves concerning them without rashness and arrogance: and consequently that the pious and just do not even have concerning these things the certainty which the Schools concede, namely moral or conjectural. And thus the dogmas of the Roman School in this part greatly disagree from the sense which its own doctors are accustomed to generate in the listening populace by their preachings.
pass_b_english: School usage itself refuses to call fixed moral judgment ‘ignorance.’
Yet popular Roman preaching of not-knowing trains hearers into suspended minds—Le Blanc’s closing charge as Certitudine ends.
